items.title: Performance of artificial intelligence versus clinician left-ventricular segmentation of cardiac MRI for mortality prediction: a retrospective, multicentre, prognostic study.
items.abstract: Ejection fraction, a key measure of cardiac function, is used in health care for clinical decision making and risk stratification. We hypothesised that a deep-learning artificial intelligence (AI) segmentation of ejection fraction obtained from cardiac MRI (CMR) outperforms expert clinician segmentation for the prediction of all-cause mortality. In this retrospective, multicentre, prognostic study, we studied a cohort of 27 382 consecutive patients who underwent cardiac MRI (CMR) in the UK and the USA. Patients were referred for CMR from nine hospitals to Barts Heart Centre (BHC), London. Patients were identified from the reporting archive at BHC as having undergone a CMR between Oct 1, 2014 and Dec 31, 2019. A further cohort of patients was also identified from University of Pittsburgh Medical Centre (UPMC), Pittsburgh, PA, USA, as having undergone a CMR between June 1, 2010 and March 31, 2016. Mortality data were obtained from national and local databases. AI segmentation was done on all CMR studies, and Cox proportional hazards models were fitted to compare the prognostic value of AI-measured versus clinician-measured left-ventricular volume metrics. Model fit was compared using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), discrimination using C indices and the incremental value of AI over clinician segmentation using likelihood-ratio tests of nested models. 27 382 patients received a baseline CMR (26 106 patients from BHC and 1276 from UPMC). The median follow-up was 5·6 years (IQR 4·4-6·9), during which 3458 (13%) of 27 382 patients died. AI ejection fraction showed better model fit (AIC 57 936 vs 58 097, ΔAIC 161 favouring AI) and marginally better discrimination (C index 0·669 vs 0·637; ΔC 0·033 [95% CI 0·026-0·041]). AI ejection fraction significantly improved model fit when added to clinician ejection fraction (χ 2 =168, p 2 =7·5, p=0·023). After adjustment for age and sex, AI-derived ejection fraction showed better model fit (AIC 55 684 vs 55 742; ΔAIC 59) and had marginally better discrimination (C index of 0·781 vs 0·777; ΔC=0·004 [95% CI 0·002-0·006]). AI-derived ejection fraction shows marginally superior prediction for mortality than clinician-derived ejection fraction in patients who had CMR. Findings support the potential utility of AI for first-line ejection-fraction measurement with clinician oversight, although this should be investigated in prospective studies. National Institute for Health and Care Research Clinical Lectureship and the British Heart Foundation Accelerator Award.

Measurement of left atrial appendage blood transport in patients with atrial fibrillation using dynamic contrast 4DCT.
items.abstract: Current stroke risk stratification in atrial fibrillation (AF) relies on clinical factors with known limitations. Blood stasis in the Left Atrial Appendage (LAA) promotes thrombus formation, contributing to embolic stroke. Our objective is to map contrast transport throughout the LAA volume with 4DCT. Patients being treated for AF underwent dynamic contrast 4DCT. Hounsfield unit (HU) vs. time curves were fitted voxel wise using gamma-variate models. Three LAA blood transport metrics were extracted: (1) increase in residence time between distal LAA voxels and the LA/LAA orifice (ΔRT); (2) ratio of peak HU enhancement in distal LAA voxels to peak HU in the LA/LAA orifice (ΔHU); and (3) total volume of delayed filling (V stasis ) in the LAA. A composite "LAA Transport Index" (LAATI) was computed using principal component analysis. Among all 93 patients, a wide range of delayed transport in the LAA was observed with: 0 ​ stasis ​ stasis ​ stasis . For patients imaged in sinus the mean LAATI ​= ​-1.06 ​± ​0.4, and for those imaged in AF the mean LAATI ​= ​0.43 ​± ​1.7. LAATI did not correlate with CHA2DS2-VASc (p ​= ​0.44) or chicken wing morphology (p ​= ​0.21). 4DCT-based voxel-wise quantification of LAA contrast transport using gamma-variate modeling is technically feasible. Further studies are required to determine its potential value for personalized stroke-risk assessment.

items.title: The impact of HFE genotypes and iron loading on joint disease: evidence for HFE-associated arthropathy without genetic haemochromatosis.
items.abstract: This study aims to determine the association of recognised HFE genotypes with arthropathy fulfilling European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) haemochromatosis arthropathy (HA) classification criteria (CC), and the contributory role of iron loading. We analysed 373 participants from the EULAR HA inception cohorts: group 1, C282Y homozygous with significant iron overload (n = 154); group 2A, C282Y homozygous without significant iron overload (n = 27); group 2B, other HFE genotypes irrespective of iron status (n = 72); group 3 (osteoarthritis/calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy controls without iron overload (n = 120). Group 2 were selected from rheumatology patients with persistent unexplained joint pain, potential HA, and/or pre-existing genotyping. Between-group comparisons and genotype-stratified analyses were performed. In group 2, associations among ferritin, transferrin saturation, and HA-CC fulfilment were assessed using regression analyses. HA-CC were fulfilled in 71.4% of group 1, 22.2% group 2A, 43.1% group 2B, and 6.7% group 3 (P < .001 all comparisons). Compared with group 3, group 2 demonstrated significantly higher prevalence of HA-CC fulfilment and 5 HA-CC features (P < .003 all items), including participants with H63D variants. Ferritin levels and transferrin saturation were not associated with HA-CC fulfilment odds ratio (OR) 1.000 per 1 µg/L increase, 95% CI: 1.000-1.001, P = .28; OR 0.98 per 1% increase, 95% CI: 0.96-1.01, P = .14, respectively). A substantial proportion of individuals without haemochromatosis but carrying HFE genotypes fulfil EULAR HA-CC, without an association with ferritin levels or transferrin saturation. This supports a potential iron-independent contribution of HFE variants to arthropathy. Although 'haemochromatosis arthropathy' is found in people with genetic haemochromatosis, 'HFE associated arthropathy without genetic haemochromatosis' describes metacarpophalangeal and/or ankle joint disease with any HFE genotype.

items.title: Corrigendum to "Microbubble-assisted pLIFU enhances riboflavin delivery and corneal cross-linking in an in vivo rabbit keratoconus-like model" [Ultrason. Sonochem. 133 (2026) 108075].
[The role of immune checkpoints in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: An emerging therapeutic paradigm].
items.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive and often fatal lung disease for which therapeutic options remain limited. Recent research has highlighted the involvement of immune checkpoints, a class of receptors that have revolutionized cancer immunotherapy, in the regulation of IPF development. This mini-review aims to summarize current knowledge on the role of these immune checkpoints in IPF, including PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4, as well as other receptors such as TIM-3, VISTA, TIGIT, LAG-3, ICOS, TREM-2, and the SIRPα/CD47 axis. Strategically targeting some of these immune checkpoints could offer a promising therapeutic approach to slow the progression of fibrosis in IPF.

items.title: Engineered nanobiotechnology for cancer immunotherapy.
items.abstract: Despite the clinical success of immune checkpoint blockade and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies, solid tumors frequently remain poorly responsive due to multi-step failures in initiating, maintaining, and executing immune responses in vivo. Overcoming these barriers requires organizing immune cues into productive biological relationships rather than simply intensifying systemic immune stimulation. This review examines how engineered nanobiotechnology addresses this central challenge by spatially and temporally coordinating key immune processes. Adopting a biology-driven and engineering-enhanced perspective, we analyze nanoscale interventions across four critical phases of antitumor immunity. Immune initiation engineering optimizes antigen processing and localized delivery to promote productive T-cell priming. To sustain these responses, targeted nanosystems reprogram lymphocytes and myeloid cells toward functional effector states in vivo. At the cellular interface, engineered platforms spatially coordinate immune recognition and effector engagement, while tumor microenvironment (TME) engineering remodels the suppressive niche to support tumor-specific immune activation. By organizing these advances through a process-centered engineering framework, we elucidate how nanobiotechnology can convert otherwise localized, transient, or poorly coordinated immune stimulation into integrated antitumor immunity. Finally, we discuss emerging clinical examples and translational requirements, highlighting how pharmacodynamic immune readouts, patient stratification, and manufacturable designs will drive next-generation nano-immunotherapies toward solid-tumor treatment.

items.title: CD39, CD73, and CD38 track tumor burden and reveal immune remodeling during mogamulizumab therapy in Sézary syndrome.
Enhanced melanoma-specific cytotoxic T-cell expansion and the clinical outcomes with simlukafusp alfa and pembrolizumab following checkpoint inhibitor progression.
Gut microbiome in immuno-oncology: potential for clinical exploitation.
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment landscape of multiple malignancies, yet durable clinical benefit remains limited to a subset of patients, while immune-related adverse events still represent a major therapeutic challenge. Over the past decade, compelling evidence has established the gut microbiota as a key host determinant of both the efficacy and toxicity of cancer immunotherapy. Given its profound diversity and plasticity, as well as its impact on systemic immunity, gut commensals are now considered as both a promising predictive biomarker of response and a potentially actionable therapeutic target. As a result, different microbiota-informed approaches are being explored for precision immune-oncology. Specifically, emerging biomarker strategies are moving beyond single bacterial taxa toward ecological and functional microbial signatures with improved reproducibility across patient cohorts. At the same time, therapeutic modulation of the gut microbiome, through dietary interventions, prebiotics, probiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation, is being actively investigated to enhance responsiveness to ICIs and mitigate immune-related adverse events. In this review, we discuss the biological mechanisms linking gut microbiota and immunotherapy, evaluate its role as biomarker and therapeutic target, and address the current challenges that need to be overcome to integrate microbiota into precision immune-oncology.

items.title: Endovascular brachytherapy using 125 I seeds strand combined with transarterial chemoembolization, lenvatinib, and camrelizumab for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma with hepatic vein tumor thrombus.
items.abstract: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of Iodine-125( 125 I) seed strand implantation in combination with transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), lenvatinib, and camrelizumab for the treatment of unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (uHCC) with hepatic vein tumor thrombus (HVTT). From January 2020 to December 2023, 76 uHCC patients with HVTT were included in this single-center retrospective study. Thirty-six patients underwent 125 I seed strand implantation combined with TACE, lenvatinib, and camrelizumab (group A), whereas 40 patients received TACE combined with lenvatinib and camrelizumab (group B). Outcome measures comprised with technique success rate, overall response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), overall survival (OS) time, progression-free survival (PFS) time, and adverse event occurrence rate. The technique was successfully performed in all patients. The mean intended dose (r, irradiation range = 10 mm; z, irradiation duration = 240 days) was 64.0 ± 0.3 Gy. No grade 3 or 4 adverse events related to 125 I seed strand implantation occurred in group A. The ORR and DCR of HVTT were significantly higher in group A compared with group B (ORR, 72.2% vs. 15.0%, p < 0.001; DCR, 88.9% vs. 35%, p < 0.001). And the median OS time and PFS time were significant longer in group A compared with group B (OS, 22.1 ± 2.4 vs. 14.0 ± 1.7 months, p < 0.001; PFS, 17.6 ± 0.3 vs. 8.0 ± 0.6 months, p < 0.001). In the multivariate Cox regression analysis, treatment regimen was an independent prognostic factor for OS. No serious complications related to interventional treatment, including acute hepatic failure, liver abscess, intraperitoneal bleeding, and radiation hepatitis was observed. 125 I seeds strand combined with TACE, lenvatinib, and camrelizumab as the treatment strategy for uHCC patients with HVTT is safe and effective.

items.title: Anticancer drug CX-5461 exerts pangenotypic anti-hepatitis E virus effect in human liver organoids and animal models.
A Case of Herpes Simplex Virus Dissemination: An Uncommon Cause of Acute Hepatitis.
Inarigivir Exhibits RIG-I-Independent Antiviral Activity Against HBV DNA Replication in vitro by Inhibiting Viral Polymerase Activity.
items.abstract: Inarigivir (SB 9200) is a linear dinucleotide antiviral drug designed to act as a RIG-I agonist, activating cellular innate immune responses. Clinical trials in hepatitis C virus (HCV) patients have confirmed the innate immune-activating antiviral activity of Inarigivir. In hepatitis B virus (HBV) patients, clinical trials using Inarigivir have demonstrated significant reductions in HBV DNA and RNA levels, although heterogeneous drug-induced liver injury has been observed at higher doses. To further explore Inarigivir's mechanism of action against HBV, we characterized its antiviral effect in various hepatocyte-derived cell lines, including transiently transfected HepG2 and Huh7 cells, inducible HBV stable cell lines HepAD38 and HepDES19, and HBV-infected human hepatocytes. Our results show that Inarigivir inhibits HBV DNA replication in a dose-dependent manner without affecting HBV RNA levels or pgRNA encapsidation. HBV RNA immunoprecipitation assays revealed that Inarigivir does not affect viral polymerase binding to pgRNA, while the in vitro endogenous polymerase reaction (EPR) assays demonstrated that Inarigivir inhibits HBV DNA synthesis catalyzed by polymerase within the capsid. Additionally, we provided several lines of evidence indicating that Inarigivir's antiviral effect is independent of the RIG-I signalling pathway in hepatocyte-derived cells. Taken together, our study demonstrates a RIG-I-independent antiviral mechanism of Inarigivir by inhibiting HBV DNA replication as a dinucleosidic non-chain-terminating reverse transcriptase inhibitor.

items.title: National survey of experiential learning program strategies for ensuring compliance with onboarding requirements.
items.abstract: The purpose of this study was to characterize the processes, systems, and personnel used by colleges and schools of pharmacy to collect, monitor, and ensure compliance with experiential education onboarding requirements. A 27-item electronic questionnaire was sent to experiential education faculty and staff at all Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education (ACPE) accredited pharmacy programs in spring 2025. Questions included demographics, general onboarding questions and resources, onboarding requirements, and strategies for increasing requirement compliance. Descriptive statistics were used to analyze multiple-choice questions, and common approaches to compliance were identified through the open-ended question. The survey had a response rate of 59.6% (84/141 programs). More than 95% of programs required hepatitis B, MMR, varicella, and Tdap vaccinations, while 90.5% required influenza vaccination. Less than 30% of programs required the COVID-19 vaccination or booster. Annual tuberculosis (TB) testing was required by 90.5% of programs. Background checks were required yearly in 63.1% of programs, and drug screening was required in 54.76% of programs. Regulatory modules and intern licenses were required by most programs. Programs used multiple compliance monitoring platforms, and consequences of non-compliance included referral to professionalism committees, course registration holds, grade deductions, or prohibition from attending rotations. Non-compliance management approaches reported include automated reminders, EE advisors, and group onboarding sessions. Experiential program onboarding requirements showed commonality regarding childhood immunizations and background checks, with variability in other requirements and compliance monitoring platforms. Regular review of requirements and employing mechanisms for ensuring compliance will assist experiential programs with student placements.

items.title: In Reply to Aydin and Kayikcioglu.
Microbiota in liver carcinogenesis: Illuminating the complex relationship.
items.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) develops predominantly in patients with cirrhosis, yet the biological mechanisms underlying the transition from cirrhosis to malignancy remain incompletely understood. Increasing evidence suggests that the oral-gut-liver axis contributes to this process through coordinated interactions among oral and intestinal microbiota, the epithelial barrier, the immune system, and the liver. While previous reviews have primarily focused on gut dysbiosis in cirrhosis and its complications, emerging evidence indicates that microbiome-associated alterations actively contribute to hepatocarcinogenesis. In this review, we propose a transition-state model in which disruption of the oral-gut-liver axis promotes progression from cirrhosis to HCC through functional microbiome insufficiency, epithelial barrier dysfunction, microbial translocation, inflammatory remodeling, and immune dysregulation. We emphasize that disruption of microbial metabolic functions, including reduced butyrate biosynthesis, bile acid remodeling, altered tryptophan metabolism, and enrichment of virulence-associated pathways may be more biologically relevant than taxonomic changes alone. We further discuss emerging biomarkers representing distinct domains of the gut-liver axis, including butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase (BCoAT) as a marker of microbial function, intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP) as a marker of epithelial injury, and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) as a marker of microbial translocation and endotoxemia. Finally, we discuss the translational implications of integrating microbiome-derived functional biomarkers with immune and clinical profiling for biological risk stratification, early detection, and precision hepatology as well as therapeutic strategies based on microbiome modulation. This framework shifts the focus from descriptive dysbiosis toward mechanistic host-microbiome interactions, highlights the oral-gut-liver axis as an active contributor to hepatocarcinogenesis, and provides a conceptual foundation for future microbiome-informed surveillance, risk stratification, and therapeutic strategies.

items.title: Circulating Tumor DNA and Cell-Free DNA as Candidate Biomarkers After Image-Guided Locoregional Therapy in Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Colorectal Liver Metastases: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: To review ctDNA and cfDNA as biomarkers after locoregional therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and colorectal liver metastases (CRLM). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched (July 2026) for ctDNA/cfDNA studies in HCC or CRLM patients undergoing TACE, Y90, or ablation; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessed risk of bias. Eleven studies were included (eight HCC, three CRLM; n≈820). Pre-treatment ctDNA mutations predicted survival after TACE (CTNNB1: HR 5.3, 95% CI 1.4-20.6; TP53: HR 5.3, 95% CI 1.4-10.1; KEAP1: HR 22.0, 95% CI 2.2-221.0). A cfDNA/ctDNA score stratified progression-free survival after TACE (1.3 vs 10.3 months; p=0.002). ctDNA predicted death after ablation in HCC (HR 2.6, 95% CI 1.5-4.7; p=0.001) and recurrence in CRLM (HR 2.97, 95% CI 1.47-6.03; P=0.003). Y90 evidence was limited. CtDNA and cfDNA correlated with treatment outcomes after locoregional therapy; evidence is heterogeneous and biomarker-driven trials are required before clinical implementation.

items.title: Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Neoplasms: Integrating WHO Classification with CT, MRI, and Molecular Imaging.
items.abstract: Pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (pNENs) are a heterogeneous group of tumors within gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (GEP-NENs), with variable clinical behavior and prognosis. The World Health Organization (WHO) classification distinguishes well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) from poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas (NECs), including the recognition of grade 3 NETs (NET G3) as a separate entity with important clinical implications. Multiphasic computed tomography (CT) and multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are central to detection, staging, and follow-up, with MRI offering superior sensitivity for liver metastases, particularly with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and hepatobiliary phase (HBP). Molecular imaging with somatostatin receptor-targeted PET and 18 F-FDG PET provides complementary biologic information by assessing receptor expression, metabolic aggressiveness, and tumor heterogeneity. SSTR-targeted PET supports confirmation of neuroendocrine phenotype, whole-body staging, and selection of candidates for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, whereas 18 F-FDG PET identifies aggressive or dedifferentiated tumor components that may influence prognosis and favor chemotherapy-oriented strategies. Despite advances, noninvasive grading remains limited, requiring integration of imaging with histopathology. An integrated multimodality approach combining CT, MRI, molecular imaging, and pathology is therefore essential for accurate staging, biopsy targeting, treatment stratification, and personalized management.
